input:
In this report, we describe a Theano-based AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012)
implementation and its naive data parallelism on multiple GPUs. Our performance
on 2 GPUs is comparable with the state-of-art Caffe library (Jia et al., 2014)
run on 1 GPU. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first open-source
Python-based AlexNet implementation to-date.
Help me polish this:
This report details a Theano-based implementation of AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) with naive multi-GPU data parallelism. Performance on two GPUs matches the state-of-the-art Caffe library (Jia et al., 2014) on a single GPU. To our knowledge, this is the first open-source, Python-based AlexNet implementation.

(Word count: 56)

input:
We show that deep narrow Boltzmann machines are universal approximators of
probability distributions on the activities of their visible units, provided
they have sufficiently many hidden layers, each containing the same number of
units as the visible layer. We show that, within certain parameter domains,
deep Boltzmann machines can be studied as feedforward networks. We provide
upper and lower bounds on the sufficient depth and width of universal
approximators. These results settle various intuitions regarding undirected
networks and, in particular, they show that deep narrow Boltzmann machines are
at least as compact universal approximators as narrow sigmoid belief networks
and restricted Boltzmann machines, with respect to the currently available
bounds for those models.
Help me polish this: We demonstrate that deep, narrow Boltzmann machines can universally approximate probability distributions over their visible units, given a sufficient number of hidden layers, each with the same width as the visible layer. Within specific parameter regimes, these models can be analyzed as feedforward networks. We establish upper and lower bounds on the depth and width required for universal approximation. These findings confirm key intuitions about undirected networks, proving that deep narrow Boltzmann machines are at least as compact as universal approximators compared to narrow sigmoid belief networks and restricted Boltzmann machines, based on the best-known bounds for those architectures.

input:
Leveraging advances in variational inference, we propose to enhance recurrent
neural networks with latent variables, resulting in Stochastic Recurrent
Networks (STORNs). The model i) can be trained with stochastic gradient
methods, ii) allows structured and multi-modal conditionals at each time step,
iii) features a reliable estimator of the marginal likelihood and iv) is a
generalisation of deterministic recurrent neural networks. We evaluate the
method on four polyphonic musical data sets and motion capture data.
Help me polish this:
Drawing on advances in variational inference, we introduce Stochastic Recurrent Networks (STORNs), which augment recurrent neural networks with latent variables. This model is trainable with stochastic gradient methods, supports structured and multi-modal per-step conditionals, provides a reliable marginal likelihood estimator, and generalizes deterministic recurrent networks. We evaluate STORNs on four polyphonic music datasets and motion capture data.

Word count: 68

input:
We describe a general framework for online adaptation of optimization
hyperparameters by `hot swapping' their values during learning. We investigate
this approach in the context of adaptive learning rate selection using an
explore-exploit strategy from the multi-armed bandit literature. Experiments on
a benchmark neural network show that the hot swapping approach leads to
consistently better solutions compared to well-known alternatives such as
AdaDelta and stochastic gradient with exhaustive hyperparameter search.
Help me polish this: We present a general framework for online hyperparameter adaptation by “hot swapping” their values during training. This approach is examined for adaptive learning rate selection using an explore-exploit strategy from multi-armed bandit literature. Benchmark neural network experiments demonstrate that hot swapping consistently achieves better solutions than established alternatives like AdaDelta and stochastic gradient descent with exhaustive hyperparameter search.

input:
Many modern multiclass and multilabel problems are characterized by
increasingly large output spaces. For these problems, label embeddings have
been shown to be a useful primitive that can improve computational and
statistical efficiency. In this work we utilize a correspondence between rank
constrained estimation and low dimensional label embeddings that uncovers a
fast label embedding algorithm which works in both the multiclass and
multilabel settings. The result is a randomized algorithm for partial least
squares, whose running time is exponentially faster than naive algorithms. We
demonstrate our techniques on two large-scale public datasets, from the Large
Scale Hierarchical Text Challenge and the Open Directory Project, where we
obtain state of the art results.
Help me polish this:
Many modern multiclass and multilabel problems involve increasingly large output spaces. For these, label embeddings have proven to be a useful primitive, improving both computational and statistical efficiency. In this work, we exploit a correspondence between rank-constrained estimation and low-dimensional label embeddings. This reveals a fast label embedding algorithm applicable to both multiclass and multilabel settings. The result is a randomized method for partial least squares, with a running time exponentially faster than naive approaches. We demonstrate our techniques on two large-scale public datasets—from the Large Scale Hierarchical Text Challenge and the Open Directory Project—achieving state-of-the-art results.

(Word count: 113)

input:
Accurate representational learning of both the explicit and implicit
relationships within data is critical to the ability of machines to perform
more complex and abstract reasoning tasks. We describe the efficient weakly
supervised learning of such inferences by our Dynamic Adaptive Network
Intelligence (DANI) model. We report state-of-the-art results for DANI over
question answering tasks in the bAbI dataset that have proved difficult for
contemporary approaches to learning representation (Weston et al., 2015).
Help me polish this:
Accurate learning of both explicit and implicit relationships in data is essential for machines to perform complex, abstract reasoning. We present the Dynamic Adaptive Network Intelligence (DANI) model, which efficiently learns such inferences through weak supervision. DANI achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging question-answering tasks from the bAbI dataset, which have proven difficult for existing representation learning methods (Weston et al., 2015).

(Word count: 73)

input:
Automatic speech recognition systems usually rely on spectral-based features,
such as MFCC of PLP. These features are extracted based on prior knowledge such
as, speech perception or/and speech production. Recently, convolutional neural
networks have been shown to be able to estimate phoneme conditional
probabilities in a completely data-driven manner, i.e. using directly temporal
raw speech signal as input. This system was shown to yield similar or better
performance than HMM/ANN based system on phoneme recognition task and on large
scale continuous speech recognition task, using less parameters. Motivated by
these studies, we investigate the use of simple linear classifier in the
CNN-based framework. Thus, the network learns linearly separable features from
raw speech. We show that such system yields similar or better performance than
MLP based system using cepstral-based features as input.
Help me polish this:
Automatic speech recognition systems traditionally rely on spectral-based features like MFCC or PLP, which are derived from prior knowledge of speech perception or production. Recently, convolutional neural networks have demonstrated the ability to estimate phoneme probabilities in a fully data-driven way, using raw temporal speech signals directly as input. Such CNN systems achieve performance comparable to or better than conventional HMM/ANN models on phoneme and large-vocabulary continuous speech recognition tasks, while using fewer parameters.

Inspired by these results, we explore the use of a simple linear classifier within a CNN-based framework. This approach enables the network to learn linearly separable features directly from raw speech. We demonstrate that this system delivers performance similar to or surpassing that of an MLP-based system using conventional cepstral features as input.

(Word count: 132)

input:
We describe the neural-network training framework used in the Kaldi speech
recognition toolkit, which is geared towards training DNNs with large amounts
of training data using multiple GPU-equipped or multi-core machines. In order
to be as hardware-agnostic as possible, we needed a way to use multiple
machines without generating excessive network traffic. Our method is to average
the neural network parameters periodically (typically every minute or two), and
redistribute the averaged parameters to the machines for further training. Each
machine sees different data. By itself, this method does not work very well.
However, we have another method, an approximate and efficient implementation of
Natural Gradient for Stochastic Gradient Descent (NG-SGD), which seems to allow
our periodic-averaging method to work well, as well as substantially improving
the convergence of SGD on a single machine.
Help me polish this: We present the neural network training framework developed for the Kaldi speech recognition toolkit. It is designed to train DNNs on large datasets across multiple GPU-equipped or multi-core machines. To remain hardware-agnostic, we required a multi-machine approach that avoids excessive network traffic. Our solution is to periodically average the neural network parameters—typically every minute or two—and redistribute the averaged parameters to all machines for continued training. Each machine processes different data. While this averaging method alone performs poorly, we combine it with an efficient, approximate implementation of Natural Gradient for Stochastic Gradient Descent (NG-SGD). This combination enables our periodic-averaging strategy to work effectively and also significantly accelerates SGD convergence on a single machine.

input:
We develop a new method for visualizing and refining the invariances of
learned representations. Specifically, we test for a general form of
invariance, linearization, in which the action of a transformation is confined
to a low-dimensional subspace. Given two reference images (typically, differing
by some transformation), we synthesize a sequence of images lying on a path
between them that is of minimal length in the space of the representation (a
"representational geodesic"). If the transformation relating the two reference
images is linearized by the representation, this sequence should follow the
gradual evolution of this transformation. We use this method to assess the
invariance properties of a state-of-the-art image classification network and
find that geodesics generated for image pairs differing by translation,
rotation, and dilation do not evolve according to their associated
transformations. Our method also suggests a remedy for these failures, and
following this prescription, we show that the modified representation is able
to linearize a variety of geometric image transformations.
Help me polish this:
We introduce a new method for visualizing and refining the invariances in learned representations. Specifically, we test for a general form of invariance called linearization, where the effect of a transformation is constrained to a low-dimensional subspace. Given two reference images—often related by a transformation—we synthesize a sequence of images that forms a minimal-length path between them in the representation space (a “representational geodesic”). If the representation linearizes the transformation, this sequence should trace its gradual progression.

Applying this method to a state-of-the-art image classifier, we find that geodesics for image pairs differing by translation, rotation, or dilation do not evolve according to the intended transformations. Our approach also suggests a corrective strategy. By implementing this modification, we demonstrate that the adjusted representation can successfully linearize a range of geometric image transformations.

(Word count: 158)

input:
Why does Deep Learning work? What representations does it capture? How do
higher-order representations emerge? We study these questions from the
perspective of group theory, thereby opening a new approach towards a theory of
Deep learning.
  One factor behind the recent resurgence of the subject is a key algorithmic
step called {\em pretraining}: first search for a good generative model for the
input samples, and repeat the process one layer at a time. We show deeper
implications of this simple principle, by establishing a connection with the
interplay of orbits and stabilizers of group actions. Although the neural
networks themselves may not form groups, we show the existence of {\em shadow}
groups whose elements serve as close approximations.
  Over the shadow groups, the pre-training step, originally introduced as a
mechanism to better initialize a network, becomes equivalent to a search for
features with minimal orbits. Intuitively, these features are in a way the {\em
simplest}. Which explains why a deep learning network learns simple features
first. Next, we show how the same principle, when repeated in the deeper
layers, can capture higher order representations, and why representation
complexity increases as the layers get deeper.
Help me polish this:
Why does deep learning work? What representations does it capture? How do higher-order features emerge? We investigate these questions through the lens of group theory, proposing a novel pathway toward a theory of deep learning.

A key driver behind the field’s resurgence is *pretraining*: first learn a generative model of the input data, then repeat this process layer by layer. We reveal a deeper significance of this principle by linking it to the interaction of orbits and stabilizers in group actions. Although neural networks themselves are not groups, we demonstrate the existence of *shadow* groups whose elements closely approximate network transformations.

Within this framework, pretraining—often viewed merely as improved initialization—becomes equivalent to searching for features with minimal orbits. Intuitively, these are the *simplest* features, explaining why networks learn basic patterns first. We then show how applying the same principle in deeper layers captures increasingly complex, higher-order representations, clarifying why representation complexity grows with network depth.

input:
We present a novel architecture, the "stacked what-where auto-encoders"
(SWWAE), which integrates discriminative and generative pathways and provides a
unified approach to supervised, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning
without relying on sampling during training. An instantiation of SWWAE uses a
convolutional net (Convnet) (LeCun et al. (1998)) to encode the input, and
employs a deconvolutional net (Deconvnet) (Zeiler et al. (2010)) to produce the
reconstruction. The objective function includes reconstruction terms that
induce the hidden states in the Deconvnet to be similar to those of the
Convnet. Each pooling layer produces two sets of variables: the "what" which
are fed to the next layer, and its complementary variable "where" that are fed
to the corresponding layer in the generative decoder.
Help me polish this:
We introduce a novel architecture called the "stacked what-where auto-encoders" (SWWAE). It unifies discriminative and generative pathways, offering a single framework for supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning—all without requiring sampling during training. In one implementation, a convolutional network (Convnet) encodes the input, while a deconvolutional network (Deconvnet) generates the reconstruction. The loss function contains reconstruction terms that encourage hidden states in the Deconvnet to resemble those in the Convnet. Each pooling layer outputs two variable sets: the "what," passed upward, and the complementary "where," sent to the matching layer in the generative decoder.

(Word count: 119)

input:
We investigate the problem of inducing word embeddings that are tailored for
a particular bilexical relation. Our learning algorithm takes an existing
lexical vector space and compresses it such that the resulting word embeddings
are good predictors for a target bilexical relation. In experiments we show
that task-specific embeddings can benefit both the quality and efficiency in
lexical prediction tasks.
Help me polish this: We investigate how to create word embeddings specifically designed for a particular bilexical relation. Our algorithm compresses an existing lexical vector space so that the resulting embeddings become strong predictors for a target relation. Experiments demonstrate that these task-specific embeddings improve both the quality and efficiency of lexical prediction tasks.

input:
A generative model is developed for deep (multi-layered) convolutional
dictionary learning. A novel probabilistic pooling operation is integrated into
the deep model, yielding efficient bottom-up (pretraining) and top-down
(refinement) probabilistic learning. Experimental results demonstrate powerful
capabilities of the model to learn multi-layer features from images, and
excellent classification results are obtained on the MNIST and Caltech 101
datasets.
Help me polish this:
A generative model is developed for deep convolutional dictionary learning. It integrates a novel probabilistic pooling operation, enabling efficient bottom-up pretraining and top-down refinement. Experiments show the model successfully learns multi-layer features from images, achieving excellent classification results on the MNIST and Caltech 101 datasets.

(58 words)

input:
Motivated by the recent progress in generative models, we introduce a model
that generates images from natural language descriptions. The proposed model
iteratively draws patches on a canvas, while attending to the relevant words in
the description. After training on Microsoft COCO, we compare our model with
several baseline generative models on image generation and retrieval tasks. We
demonstrate that our model produces higher quality samples than other
approaches and generates images with novel scene compositions corresponding to
previously unseen captions in the dataset.
Help me polish this:
Drawing on recent advances in generative models, we present a model that creates images from textual descriptions. It iteratively renders patches onto a canvas, guided by an attention mechanism over the input words. Trained on Microsoft COCO, our model is evaluated against several baselines on generation and retrieval tasks. Results show it produces higher-quality samples and can generate novel, coherent scene compositions for captions not encountered during training.

(Word count: 77)

input:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) work well on large datasets. But
labelled data is hard to collect, and in some applications larger amounts of
data are not available. The problem then is how to use CNNs with small data --
as CNNs overfit quickly. We present an efficient Bayesian CNN, offering better
robustness to over-fitting on small data than traditional approaches. This is
by placing a probability distribution over the CNN's kernels. We approximate
our model's intractable posterior with Bernoulli variational distributions,
requiring no additional model parameters.
  On the theoretical side, we cast dropout network training as approximate
inference in Bayesian neural networks. This allows us to implement our model
using existing tools in deep learning with no increase in time complexity,
while highlighting a negative result in the field. We show a considerable
improvement in classification accuracy compared to standard techniques and
improve on published state-of-the-art results for CIFAR-10.
Help me polish this:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel with large datasets, yet labeled data is often scarce, and many applications lack sufficient volumes. The challenge is to effectively employ CNNs with limited data, as they are prone to overfitting. We introduce an efficient Bayesian CNN that enhances robustness against over-fitting on small datasets compared to conventional methods. This is achieved by assigning a probability distribution over the network’s kernels. We approximate the model’s intractable posterior using Bernoulli variational distributions, which introduces no extra parameters.

Theoretically, we frame dropout training as approximate inference in Bayesian neural networks. This perspective enables implementation with existing deep learning tools without increasing time complexity, while also revealing a key limitation in the field. Experimentally, our approach yields a significant improvement in classification accuracy over standard techniques and advances the state-of-the-art on CIFAR-10.

(Word count: 149)

input:
We propose a new method for creating computationally efficient convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) by using low-rank representations of convolutional
filters. Rather than approximating filters in previously-trained networks with
more efficient versions, we learn a set of small basis filters from scratch;
during training, the network learns to combine these basis filters into more
complex filters that are discriminative for image classification. To train such
networks, a novel weight initialization scheme is used. This allows effective
initialization of connection weights in convolutional layers composed of groups
of differently-shaped filters. We validate our approach by applying it to
several existing CNN architectures and training these networks from scratch
using the CIFAR, ILSVRC and MIT Places datasets. Our results show similar or
higher accuracy than conventional CNNs with much less compute. Applying our
method to an improved version of VGG-11 network using global max-pooling, we
achieve comparable validation accuracy using 41% less compute and only 24% of
the original VGG-11 model parameters; another variant of our method gives a 1
percentage point increase in accuracy over our improved VGG-11 model, giving a
top-5 center-crop validation accuracy of 89.7% while reducing computation by
16% relative to the original VGG-11 model. Applying our method to the GoogLeNet
architecture for ILSVRC, we achieved comparable accuracy with 26% less compute
and 41% fewer model parameters. Applying our method to a near state-of-the-art
network for CIFAR, we achieved comparable accuracy with 46% less compute and
55% fewer parameters.
Help me polish this:
We propose a new method for constructing computationally efficient convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by employing low-rank representations of convolutional filters. Instead of approximating pre-trained filters, we learn a compact set of small basis filters from scratch. During training, the network learns to combine these basis filters into more complex, discriminative filters for image classification. A novel weight initialization scheme enables effective training of convolutional layers composed of groups of differently-shaped filters.

We validate our approach by applying it to several established CNN architectures, training them from scratch on the CIFAR, ILSVRC, and MIT Places datasets. Results demonstrate similar or superior accuracy to conventional CNNs with significantly reduced computation. For instance, when applied to an enhanced VGG-11 network using global max-pooling, our method achieves comparable validation accuracy while using 41% less computation and only 24% of the original parameters. Another variant improves accuracy by one percentage point over this enhanced VGG-11, attaining a top-5 center-crop validation accuracy of 89.7% on ILSVRC, with a 16% reduction in computation compared to the original VGG-11.

Applied to GoogLeNet for ILSVRC, our method yields comparable accuracy with 26% less computation and 41% fewer parameters. For a near state-of-the-art network on CIFAR, it maintains comparable accuracy while reducing computation by 46% and parameters by 55%.

(Word count: 242)

input:
Distributed representations of words have boosted the performance of many
Natural Language Processing tasks. However, usually only one representation per
word is obtained, not acknowledging the fact that some words have multiple
meanings. This has a negative effect on the individual word representations and
the language model as a whole. In this paper we present a simple model that
enables recent techniques for building word vectors to represent distinct
senses of polysemic words. In our assessment of this model we show that it is
able to effectively discriminate between words' senses and to do so in a
computationally efficient manner.
Help me polish this: Distributed word representations have significantly advanced many Natural Language Processing tasks. Typically, however, only a single representation is learned per word, ignoring the fact that many words carry multiple meanings. This limitation degrades the quality of individual word vectors and the overall language model. We introduce a straightforward model that allows modern word-embedding techniques to capture distinct senses of polysemous words. Our evaluation demonstrates that this model effectively discriminates between different word senses while remaining computationally efficient.

input:
We propose Diverse Embedding Neural Network (DENN), a novel architecture for
language models (LMs). A DENNLM projects the input word history vector onto
multiple diverse low-dimensional sub-spaces instead of a single
higher-dimensional sub-space as in conventional feed-forward neural network
LMs. We encourage these sub-spaces to be diverse during network training
through an augmented loss function. Our language modeling experiments on the
Penn Treebank data set show the performance benefit of using a DENNLM.
Help me polish this:
We introduce the Diverse Embedding Neural Network (DENN), a new architecture for language models. Unlike conventional feed-forward neural network LMs, which project the input word history into a single higher-dimensional subspace, a DENNLM projects it into multiple diverse low-dimensional subspaces. An augmented loss function encourages subspace diversity during training. Experiments on the Penn Treebank dataset demonstrate the performance advantages of a DENNLM.

(Word count: 73)

input:
A standard approach to Collaborative Filtering (CF), i.e. prediction of user
ratings on items, relies on Matrix Factorization techniques. Representations
for both users and items are computed from the observed ratings and used for
prediction. Unfortunatly, these transductive approaches cannot handle the case
of new users arriving in the system, with no known rating, a problem known as
user cold-start. A common approach in this context is to ask these incoming
users for a few initialization ratings. This paper presents a model to tackle
this twofold problem of (i) finding good questions to ask, (ii) building
efficient representations from this small amount of information. The model can
also be used in a more standard (warm) context. Our approach is evaluated on
the classical CF problem and on the cold-start problem on four different
datasets showing its ability to improve baseline performance in both cases.
Help me polish this:
A standard approach to Collaborative Filtering (CF)—predicting user ratings for items—relies on Matrix Factorization. This method computes representations for users and items from observed ratings and uses them for predictions. Unfortunately, these transductive techniques cannot handle new users who enter the system without any known ratings, a problem known as user cold-start. A common solution is to ask new users for a few initial ratings. This paper introduces a model designed to address the dual challenge of (i) selecting effective questions to ask, and (ii) constructing accurate user representations from this limited data. The model can also be applied in standard (warm) recommendation settings. We evaluate our approach on the classical CF task and on the cold-start problem across four datasets, demonstrating improved performance over baselines in both scenarios.

(Word count: 144)

input:
We propose a deep learning framework for modeling complex high-dimensional
densities called Non-linear Independent Component Estimation (NICE). It is
based on the idea that a good representation is one in which the data has a
distribution that is easy to model. For this purpose, a non-linear
deterministic transformation of the data is learned that maps it to a latent
space so as to make the transformed data conform to a factorized distribution,
i.e., resulting in independent latent variables. We parametrize this
transformation so that computing the Jacobian determinant and inverse transform
is trivial, yet we maintain the ability to learn complex non-linear
transformations, via a composition of simple building blocks, each based on a
deep neural network. The training criterion is simply the exact log-likelihood,
which is tractable. Unbiased ancestral sampling is also easy. We show that this
approach yields good generative models on four image datasets and can be used
for inpainting.
Help me polish this:
We propose a deep learning framework for modeling complex high-dimensional probability densities, called Non-linear Independent Component Estimation (NICE). The core idea is that a useful data representation should have a distribution that is simple to model. Accordingly, the method learns a non-linear, deterministic transformation that maps input data into a latent space. This transformation is designed so that the resulting latent variables follow a factorized distribution—meaning they become statistically independent.

The transformation is carefully parameterized: computing the Jacobian determinant and the inverse transformation is straightforward, yet the overall model can still learn highly complex non-linear mappings. This is achieved by composing multiple simple building blocks, each constructed from a deep neural network. Training directly maximizes the exact log-likelihood, which remains tractable. Unbiased ancestral sampling from the model is equally simple.

We demonstrate that this approach produces effective generative models on four image datasets and can also be applied to tasks such as inpainting.

input:
We introduce Deep Linear Discriminant Analysis (DeepLDA) which learns
linearly separable latent representations in an end-to-end fashion. Classic LDA
extracts features which preserve class separability and is used for
dimensionality reduction for many classification problems. The central idea of
this paper is to put LDA on top of a deep neural network. This can be seen as a
non-linear extension of classic LDA. Instead of maximizing the likelihood of
target labels for individual samples, we propose an objective function that
pushes the network to produce feature distributions which: (a) have low
variance within the same class and (b) high variance between different classes.
Our objective is derived from the general LDA eigenvalue problem and still
allows to train with stochastic gradient descent and back-propagation. For
evaluation we test our approach on three different benchmark datasets (MNIST,
CIFAR-10 and STL-10). DeepLDA produces competitive results on MNIST and
CIFAR-10 and outperforms a network trained with categorical cross entropy (same
architecture) on a supervised setting of STL-10.
Help me polish this:
We introduce Deep Linear Discriminant Analysis (DeepLDA), a method for learning linearly separable latent representations in an end-to-end fashion. While classic LDA extracts features that preserve class separability for dimensionality reduction, our core contribution is to place an LDA objective atop a deep neural network. This constitutes a non-linear extension of traditional LDA. Rather than maximizing the likelihood of individual sample labels, we propose an objective function that guides the network to produce feature distributions with: (a) low variance within each class, and (b) high variance between different classes. Derived from the general LDA eigenvalue problem, our objective remains compatible with training via stochastic gradient descent and back-propagation. We evaluate our approach on three benchmark datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and STL-10. DeepLDA yields competitive results on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and outperforms an identically structured network trained with categorical cross-entropy on the supervised setting of STL-10.

(Word count: 164)

input:
Layer-sequential unit-variance (LSUV) initialization - a simple method for
weight initialization for deep net learning - is proposed. The method consists
of the two steps. First, pre-initialize weights of each convolution or
inner-product layer with orthonormal matrices. Second, proceed from the first
to the final layer, normalizing the variance of the output of each layer to be
equal to one.
  Experiment with different activation functions (maxout, ReLU-family, tanh)
show that the proposed initialization leads to learning of very deep nets that
(i) produces networks with test accuracy better or equal to standard methods
and (ii) is at least as fast as the complex schemes proposed specifically for
very deep nets such as FitNets (Romero et al. (2015)) and Highway (Srivastava
et al. (2015)).
  Performance is evaluated on GoogLeNet, CaffeNet, FitNets and Residual nets
and the state-of-the-art, or very close to it, is achieved on the MNIST,
CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet datasets.
Help me polish this:
This paper proposes Layer-sequential unit-variance (LSUV) initialization, a straightforward method for initializing weights in deep neural networks. The technique involves two key steps. First, the weights of each convolutional or fully-connected layer are pre-initialized using orthonormal matrices. Second, proceeding sequentially from the first to the final layer, the variance of each layer's output is normalized to one.

Experiments with various activation functions—including maxout, the ReLU family, and tanh—demonstrate that this initialization enables the effective training of very deep networks. The resulting models achieve test accuracy that matches or surpasses standard methods. Furthermore, the learning process is at least as fast as with more complex, specialized schemes like FitNets and Highway networks.

Evaluations on architectures such as GoogLeNet, CaffeNet, FitNets, and Residual nets show that LSUV initialization achieves state-of-the-art, or near state-of-the-art, performance on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets.

(Word count: 150)

input:
We introduce a parametric nonlinear transformation that is well-suited for
Gaussianizing data from natural images. The data are linearly transformed, and
each component is then normalized by a pooled activity measure, computed by
exponentiating a weighted sum of rectified and exponentiated components and a
constant. We optimize the parameters of the full transformation (linear
transform, exponents, weights, constant) over a database of natural images,
directly minimizing the negentropy of the responses. The optimized
transformation substantially Gaussianizes the data, achieving a significantly
smaller mutual information between transformed components than alternative
methods including ICA and radial Gaussianization. The transformation is
differentiable and can be efficiently inverted, and thus induces a density
model on images. We show that samples of this model are visually similar to
samples of natural image patches. We demonstrate the use of the model as a
prior probability density that can be used to remove additive noise. Finally,
we show that the transformation can be cascaded, with each layer optimized
using the same Gaussianization objective, thus offering an unsupervised method
of optimizing a deep network architecture.
Help me polish this:
We introduce a parametric nonlinear transformation designed to Gaussianize natural image data. First, the data undergoes a linear transformation. Then, each component is normalized by a pooled activity measure, which is computed by exponentiating a weighted sum of rectified and exponentiated components plus a constant. We optimize all parameters of this transformation—including the linear transform, exponents, weights, and constant—over a natural image database by directly minimizing the negentropy of the responses.

The optimized transformation substantially Gaussianizes the data, achieving significantly lower mutual information between transformed components than alternative methods such as ICA and radial Gaussianization. The transformation is differentiable and efficiently invertible, thereby inducing a tractable density model on images. Samples from this model are visually similar to natural image patches. We demonstrate its utility as a prior probability density for additive noise removal. Finally, we show the transformation can be cascaded, with each layer optimized using the same Gaussianization objective, providing an unsupervised method for training a deep network architecture.

input:
We present flattened convolutional neural networks that are designed for fast
feedforward execution. The redundancy of the parameters, especially weights of
the convolutional filters in convolutional neural networks has been extensively
studied and different heuristics have been proposed to construct a low rank
basis of the filters after training. In this work, we train flattened networks
that consist of consecutive sequence of one-dimensional filters across all
directions in 3D space to obtain comparable performance as conventional
convolutional networks. We tested flattened model on different datasets and
found that the flattened layer can effectively substitute for the 3D filters
without loss of accuracy. The flattened convolution pipelines provide around
two times speed-up during feedforward pass compared to the baseline model due
to the significant reduction of learning parameters. Furthermore, the proposed
method does not require efforts in manual tuning or post processing once the
model is trained.
Help me polish this:
We introduce flattened convolutional neural networks, optimized for rapid feedforward execution. Prior research has extensively examined the redundancy in convolutional filter weights, proposing various heuristics to derive low-rank filter bases after training. In contrast, this work directly trains flattened networks composed of consecutive one-dimensional filters applied across all spatial directions. This design achieves performance comparable to conventional 3D convolutional networks.

Evaluated across multiple datasets, the flattened layer effectively replaces standard 3D filters without sacrificing accuracy. The architecture reduces learnable parameters significantly, yielding approximately a two-fold speed-up in the feedforward pass compared to the baseline model. Additionally, the proposed method requires no manual tuning or post-processing after training, offering an efficient and streamlined alternative.

In this paper, we introduce a novel deep learning framework, termed Purine.
In Purine, a deep network is expressed as a bipartite graph (bi-graph), which
is composed of interconnected operators and data tensors. With the bi-graph
abstraction, networks are easily solvable with event-driven task dispatcher. We
then demonstrate that different parallelism schemes over GPUs and/or CPUs on
single or multiple PCs can be universally implemented by graph composition.
This eases researchers from coding for various parallelization schemes, and the
same dispatcher can be used for solving variant graphs. Scheduled by the task
dispatcher, memory transfers are fully overlapped with other computations,
which greatly reduce the communication overhead and help us achieve approximate
linear acceleration.
Help me polish this:
In this paper, we present a novel deep learning framework called Purine. Within Purine, a neural network is represented as a bipartite graph, consisting of interconnected operators and data tensors. This bi-graph abstraction allows networks to be executed efficiently by an event-driven task dispatcher. We show that diverse parallelism strategies—across GPUs and CPUs, on single or multiple machines—can be uniformly realized through graph composition. This frees researchers from implementing different parallelization schemes manually, while the same dispatcher can solve various graph configurations. By scheduling tasks, memory transfers are fully overlapped with computation, significantly reducing communication overhead and enabling near-linear acceleration.

input:
In this paper we propose a model that combines the strengths of RNNs and
SGVB: the Variational Recurrent Auto-Encoder (VRAE). Such a model can be used
for efficient, large scale unsupervised learning on time series data, mapping
the time series data to a latent vector representation. The model is
generative, such that data can be generated from samples of the latent space.
An important contribution of this work is that the model can make use of
unlabeled data in order to facilitate supervised training of RNNs by
initialising the weights and network state.
Help me polish this: In this paper, we propose the Variational Recurrent Auto-Encoder (VRAE), a model that integrates the capabilities of RNNs and the Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes (SGVB) framework. Designed for efficient, large-scale unsupervised learning on time series, it maps sequences to a latent vector representation. The model is generative, allowing data to be synthesized from latent space samples. A key contribution is its ability to leverage unlabeled data to support supervised RNN training by initializing network weights and hidden states.

input:
Current work in lexical distributed representations maps each word to a point
vector in low-dimensional space. Mapping instead to a density provides many
interesting advantages, including better capturing uncertainty about a
representation and its relationships, expressing asymmetries more naturally
than dot product or cosine similarity, and enabling more expressive
parameterization of decision boundaries. This paper advocates for density-based
distributed embeddings and presents a method for learning representations in
the space of Gaussian distributions. We compare performance on various word
embedding benchmarks, investigate the ability of these embeddings to model
entailment and other asymmetric relationships, and explore novel properties of
the representation.
Help me polish this: Current research in distributed lexical representations typically maps each word to a single point in a low-dimensional space. We propose instead mapping words to probability densities. This approach offers several advantages: it naturally captures uncertainty in a representation and its relationships, expresses asymmetric associations more effectively than dot-product or cosine measures, and allows for more expressive parameterizations of decision boundaries. Advocating for density-based embeddings, this paper introduces a method for learning representations as Gaussian distributions. We evaluate performance on standard word embedding benchmarks, examine the modeling of entailment and other asymmetric relations, and explore novel properties of the representation.

input:
Multipliers are the most space and power-hungry arithmetic operators of the
digital implementation of deep neural networks. We train a set of
state-of-the-art neural networks (Maxout networks) on three benchmark datasets:
MNIST, CIFAR-10 and SVHN. They are trained with three distinct formats:
floating point, fixed point and dynamic fixed point. For each of those datasets
and for each of those formats, we assess the impact of the precision of the
multiplications on the final error after training. We find that very low
precision is sufficient not just for running trained networks but also for
training them. For example, it is possible to train Maxout networks with 10
bits multiplications.
Help me polish this:
Multipliers are the most space- and power-intensive arithmetic operators in the digital implementation of deep neural networks. We train state-of-the-art Maxout networks on three benchmark datasets—MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN—using three numerical formats: floating point, fixed point, and dynamic fixed point. For each dataset and format, we evaluate how multiplication precision affects the final error after training. Our results show that very low precision is sufficient not only for inference but also for training. For instance, Maxout networks can be trained successfully using only 10-bit multiplications.

(Word count: 100)

input:
Multiple instance learning (MIL) can reduce the need for costly annotation in
tasks such as semantic segmentation by weakening the required degree of
supervision. We propose a novel MIL formulation of multi-class semantic
segmentation learning by a fully convolutional network. In this setting, we
seek to learn a semantic segmentation model from just weak image-level labels.
The model is trained end-to-end to jointly optimize the representation while
disambiguating the pixel-image label assignment. Fully convolutional training
accepts inputs of any size, does not need object proposal pre-processing, and
offers a pixelwise loss map for selecting latent instances. Our multi-class MIL
loss exploits the further supervision given by images with multiple labels. We
evaluate this approach through preliminary experiments on the PASCAL VOC
segmentation challenge.
Help me polish this:
Multiple instance learning (MIL) reduces the need for costly annotation in tasks like semantic segmentation by relaxing the required level of supervision. We introduce a novel MIL formulation for multi-class semantic segmentation using a fully convolutional network. This approach enables learning a segmentation model from only image-level labels. The model is trained end-to-end to simultaneously optimize its internal representation and resolve the assignment of pixel-level labels from image-level tags. Fully convolutional training accepts inputs of any size, eliminates the need for object proposal preprocessing, and provides a pixelwise loss map for identifying latent instances. Our multi-class MIL loss additionally leverages the richer supervision available in images with multiple labels. We assess the method through initial experiments on the PASCAL VOC segmentation benchmark.

(Word count: 124)

input:
Recently, nested dropout was proposed as a method for ordering representation
units in autoencoders by their information content, without diminishing
reconstruction cost. However, it has only been applied to training
fully-connected autoencoders in an unsupervised setting. We explore the impact
of nested dropout on the convolutional layers in a CNN trained by
backpropagation, investigating whether nested dropout can provide a simple and
systematic way to determine the optimal representation size with respect to the
desired accuracy and desired task and data complexity.
Help me polish this: Recently, nested dropout was introduced to order representation units in autoencoders by information content, without degrading reconstruction quality. However, it has only been used with fully-connected autoencoders in unsupervised learning. We study the effect of nested dropout on convolutional layers within a CNN trained via backpropagation. Our goal is to determine whether this method offers a straightforward, systematic approach for selecting the optimal representation size, based on target accuracy and the complexity of the task and data.

input:
Stochastic gradient algorithms have been the main focus of large-scale
learning problems and they led to important successes in machine learning. The
convergence of SGD depends on the careful choice of learning rate and the
amount of the noise in stochastic estimates of the gradients. In this paper, we
propose a new adaptive learning rate algorithm, which utilizes curvature
information for automatically tuning the learning rates. The information about
the element-wise curvature of the loss function is estimated from the local
statistics of the stochastic first order gradients. We further propose a new
variance reduction technique to speed up the convergence. In our preliminary
experiments with deep neural networks, we obtained better performance compared
to the popular stochastic gradient algorithms.
Help me polish this: Stochastic gradient methods are central to large-scale machine learning and have driven many of its successes. However, SGD's convergence relies heavily on a well-chosen learning rate and is sensitive to noise in the gradient estimates. This paper introduces a novel adaptive learning rate algorithm that automates tuning by incorporating curvature information. This per-parameter curvature is estimated efficiently from the local statistics of past stochastic gradients. We further enhance the method with a new variance reduction technique to accelerate convergence. In preliminary experiments on deep neural networks, our approach outperformed established stochastic gradient algorithms.

input:
When a three-dimensional object moves relative to an observer, a change
occurs on the observer's image plane and in the visual representation computed
by a learned model. Starting with the idea that a good visual representation is
one that transforms linearly under scene motions, we show, using the theory of
group representations, that any such representation is equivalent to a
combination of the elementary irreducible representations. We derive a striking
relationship between irreducibility and the statistical dependency structure of
the representation, by showing that under restricted conditions, irreducible
representations are decorrelated. Under partial observability, as induced by
the perspective projection of a scene onto the image plane, the motion group
does not have a linear action on the space of images, so that it becomes
necessary to perform inference over a latent representation that does transform
linearly. This idea is demonstrated in a model of rotating NORB objects that
employs a latent representation of the non-commutative 3D rotation group SO(3).
Help me polish this:
When a three-dimensional object moves relative to an observer, the image seen by the observer—and the internal representation formed by a learned model—also changes. We propose that a strong visual representation should transform linearly under such scene motions. Using group representation theory, we demonstrate that any linear representation is equivalent to a combination of fundamental, irreducible representations. A notable connection emerges: under certain conditions, these irreducible representations become statistically decorrelated, linking algebraic structure to dependency.

Because perspective projection makes the motion group act nonlinearly on image pixels, we must instead perform inference on a latent representation that does transform linearly. We illustrate this principle with a model of rotating NORB objects, employing a latent representation based on the non-commutative 3D rotation group, SO(3).

(Word count: 160)

input:
Efficient Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is an important task that has a
wide applicability in recommendation systems and classification with a large
number of classes. Solutions based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) as well
as tree-based solutions have been investigated in the recent literature, to
perform approximate MIPS in sublinear time. In this paper, we compare these to
another extremely simple approach for solving approximate MIPS, based on
variants of the k-means clustering algorithm. Specifically, we propose to train
a spherical k-means, after having reduced the MIPS problem to a Maximum Cosine
Similarity Search (MCSS). Experiments on two standard recommendation system
benchmarks as well as on large vocabulary word embeddings, show that this
simple approach yields much higher speedups, for the same retrieval precision,
than current state-of-the-art hashing-based and tree-based methods. This simple
method also yields more robust retrievals when the query is corrupted by noise.
Help me polish this:
Efficient Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) is crucial for applications like recommendation systems and large-scale classification. Recent work has developed sublinear-time approximate solutions, primarily using locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) or tree-based methods. This paper compares those approaches to a much simpler alternative based on *k*-means clustering. We first reduce MIPS to a Maximum Cosine Similarity Search (MCSS) problem, then solve it using spherical *k*-means. Evaluated on two standard recommendation benchmarks and large word embedding datasets, this straightforward method achieves significantly higher speedups at equivalent precision compared to state-of-the-art hashing and tree techniques. It also proves more robust when queries are corrupted by noise.

**(Word count: 146)**

input:
The variational autoencoder (VAE; Kingma, Welling (2014)) is a recently
proposed generative model pairing a top-down generative network with a
bottom-up recognition network which approximates posterior inference. It
typically makes strong assumptions about posterior inference, for instance that
the posterior distribution is approximately factorial, and that its parameters
can be approximated with nonlinear regression from the observations. As we show
empirically, the VAE objective can lead to overly simplified representations
which fail to use the network's entire modeling capacity. We present the
importance weighted autoencoder (IWAE), a generative model with the same
architecture as the VAE, but which uses a strictly tighter log-likelihood lower
bound derived from importance weighting. In the IWAE, the recognition network
uses multiple samples to approximate the posterior, giving it increased
flexibility to model complex posteriors which do not fit the VAE modeling
assumptions. We show empirically that IWAEs learn richer latent space
representations than VAEs, leading to improved test log-likelihood on density
estimation benchmarks.
Help me polish this:
The variational autoencoder (VAE; Kingma & Welling, 2014) is a generative model that combines a top-down generative network with a bottom-up recognition network for approximate posterior inference. It relies on strong assumptions, such as a factorial posterior distribution and parameters that can be approximated via nonlinear regression from data. As we demonstrate empirically, these limitations can cause the VAE objective to produce oversimplified representations that underuse the model’s capacity.

We introduce the importance weighted autoencoder (IWAE), a model with the same architecture as the VAE but employing a tighter log-likelihood lower bound derived from importance weighting. In the IWAE, the recognition network uses multiple samples to approximate the posterior, granting greater flexibility to capture complex posteriors beyond the VAE’s restrictive assumptions. Empirically, we show that IWAEs learn richer latent representations than VAEs, resulting in higher test log-likelihood on standard density estimation benchmarks.

(Word count: 159)

input:
This work investigates how using reduced precision data in Convolutional
Neural Networks (CNNs) affects network accuracy during classification. More
specifically, this study considers networks where each layer may use different
precision data. Our key result is the observation that the tolerance of CNNs to
reduced precision data not only varies across networks, a well established
observation, but also within networks. Tuning precision per layer is appealing
as it could enable energy and performance improvements. In this paper we study
how error tolerance across layers varies and propose a method for finding a low
precision configuration for a network while maintaining high accuracy. A
diverse set of CNNs is analyzed showing that compared to a conventional
implementation using a 32-bit floating-point representation for all layers, and
with less than 1% loss in relative accuracy, the data footprint required by
these networks can be reduced by an average of 74% and up to 92%.
Help me polish this:
This study examines the impact of reduced numerical precision on the classification accuracy of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Specifically, it explores configurations where each network layer can employ a different precision level. A key finding is that tolerance to precision reduction not only differs between networks—a known phenomenon—but also varies significantly *within* a single network across its layers.

This per-layer variability makes precision tuning an attractive approach for potential gains in energy efficiency and computational performance. We analyze how error tolerance differs across layers and introduce a method to identify low-precision configurations that preserve high accuracy. Evaluating a diverse set of CNNs shows that, compared to a baseline using 32-bit floating-point representation throughout, our approach reduces the data footprint by an average of 74%—and up to 92%—with less than a 1% relative drop in accuracy.

**Changes made:**

- Combined related ideas for smoother transitions.  
- Strengthened phrasing (e.g., "key finding," "introduce a method").  
- Maintained the original numerical results and emphasis on per-layer tuning.

input:
The efficiency of graph-based semi-supervised algorithms depends on the graph
of instances on which they are applied. The instances are often in a vectorial
form before a graph linking them is built. The construction of the graph relies
on a metric over the vectorial space that help define the weight of the
connection between entities. The classic choice for this metric is usually a
distance measure or a similarity measure based on the euclidean norm. We claim
that in some cases the euclidean norm on the initial vectorial space might not
be the more appropriate to solve the task efficiently. We propose an algorithm
that aims at learning the most appropriate vectorial representation for
building a graph on which the task at hand is solved efficiently.
Help me polish this:
The performance of graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithms is fundamentally tied to the quality of the underlying instance graph. Typically, instances are first provided in a vector format, and a graph is constructed by connecting them using a metric that defines the edge weights. The standard choice for this metric is often a distance or similarity measure based on the Euclidean norm. We argue, however, that this default Euclidean metric may not always be the most effective for the specific learning task. To address this, we introduce an algorithm designed to learn an optimal vectorial representation. This learned representation facilitates the construction of a graph on which the target task can be solved with greater efficiency.

**(Word count: 126)**

input:
Hypernymy, textual entailment, and image captioning can be seen as special
cases of a single visual-semantic hierarchy over words, sentences, and images.
In this paper we advocate for explicitly modeling the partial order structure
of this hierarchy. Towards this goal, we introduce a general method for
learning ordered representations, and show how it can be applied to a variety
of tasks involving images and language. We show that the resulting
representations improve performance over current approaches for hypernym
prediction and image-caption retrieval.
Help me polish this:
Hypernymy, textual entailment, and image captioning are all special cases of a unified visual-semantic hierarchy spanning words, sentences, and images. This paper argues for directly modeling the partial order inherent in this hierarchy. To that end, we introduce a general method for learning ordered representations and demonstrate its application to diverse vision-language tasks. Our approach yields representations that outperform current methods in both hypernym prediction and image-caption retrieval.

(Word count: 75)

input:
We propose local distributional smoothness (LDS), a new notion of smoothness
for statistical model that can be used as a regularization term to promote the
smoothness of the model distribution. We named the LDS based regularization as
virtual adversarial training (VAT). The LDS of a model at an input datapoint is
defined as the KL-divergence based robustness of the model distribution against
local perturbation around the datapoint. VAT resembles adversarial training,
but distinguishes itself in that it determines the adversarial direction from
the model distribution alone without using the label information, making it
applicable to semi-supervised learning. The computational cost for VAT is
relatively low. For neural network, the approximated gradient of the LDS can be
computed with no more than three pairs of forward and back propagations. When
we applied our technique to supervised and semi-supervised learning for the
MNIST dataset, it outperformed all the training methods other than the current
state of the art method, which is based on a highly advanced generative model.
We also applied our method to SVHN and NORB, and confirmed our method's
superior performance over the current state of the art semi-supervised method
applied to these datasets.
Help me polish this:
We propose **local distributional smoothness (LDS)**, a novel measure of smoothness for statistical models that can serve as a regularization term to encourage smoother model distributions. The regularization method based on LDS is termed **virtual adversarial training (VAT)**. LDS at a given input datapoint is defined as the robustness of the model distribution—measured by KL-divergence—against local perturbations around that point. Although VAT resembles adversarial training, it differs by determining the adversarial direction solely from the model distribution, without using label information. This makes VAT suitable for semi-supervised learning.

The computational cost of VAT is relatively low. For neural networks, the approximate gradient of LDS can be computed with no more than three pairs of forward and backward propagations. When applied to supervised and semi-supervised learning on the MNIST dataset, our method outperformed all existing approaches except the current state-of-the-art, which relies on a highly advanced generative model. We further evaluated VAT on SVHN and NORB datasets, where it demonstrated superior performance over the leading semi-supervised methods applied to these benchmarks.

---

**Word count:** 194

input:
The availability of large labeled datasets has allowed Convolutional Network
models to achieve impressive recognition results. However, in many settings
manual annotation of the data is impractical; instead our data has noisy
labels, i.e. there is some freely available label for each image which may or
may not be accurate. In this paper, we explore the performance of
discriminatively-trained Convnets when trained on such noisy data. We introduce
an extra noise layer into the network which adapts the network outputs to match
the noisy label distribution. The parameters of this noise layer can be
estimated as part of the training process and involve simple modifications to
current training infrastructures for deep networks. We demonstrate the
approaches on several datasets, including large scale experiments on the
ImageNet classification benchmark.
Help me polish this: Convolutional Neural Networks have achieved impressive recognition results by leveraging large, manually labeled datasets. However, in many practical scenarios, such detailed annotation is infeasible. Instead, we often have access only to data with noisy labels—freely available tags that may be inaccurate. This paper investigates the performance of discriminatively-trained ConvNets when learning from such imperfect data. We propose integrating an extra noise layer into the network architecture, which adapts the model’s outputs to align with the noisy label distribution. The parameters of this layer can be estimated seamlessly during training, requiring only simple modifications to existing deep learning frameworks. We validate our method across several datasets, including large-scale experiments on the ImageNet classification benchmark.

input:
We provide novel guaranteed approaches for training feedforward neural
networks with sparse connectivity. We leverage on the techniques developed
previously for learning linear networks and show that they can also be
effectively adopted to learn non-linear networks. We operate on the moments
involving label and the score function of the input, and show that their
factorization provably yields the weight matrix of the first layer of a deep
network under mild conditions. In practice, the output of our method can be
employed as effective initializers for gradient descent.
Help me polish this:
We introduce novel, guaranteed methods for training feedforward neural networks with sparse connectivity. Building on prior techniques for learning linear networks, we demonstrate their effective adaptation to nonlinear networks. By analyzing moments that involve the label and the input’s score function, we prove that factorizing these moments recovers the first-layer weight matrix under mild conditions. In practice, our output serves as an effective initializer for gradient descent.

(Word count: 80)

input:
Discourse relations bind smaller linguistic elements into coherent texts.
However, automatically identifying discourse relations is difficult, because it
requires understanding the semantics of the linked sentences. A more subtle
challenge is that it is not enough to represent the meaning of each sentence of
a discourse relation, because the relation may depend on links between
lower-level elements, such as entity mentions. Our solution computes
distributional meaning representations by composition up the syntactic parse
tree. A key difference from previous work on compositional distributional
semantics is that we also compute representations for entity mentions, using a
novel downward compositional pass. Discourse relations are predicted not only
from the distributional representations of the sentences, but also of their
coreferent entity mentions. The resulting system obtains substantial
improvements over the previous state-of-the-art in predicting implicit
discourse relations in the Penn Discourse Treebank.
Help me polish this:
Discourse relations combine smaller linguistic units into coherent texts. Automatically identifying these relations is challenging, as it requires understanding the semantics of the connected sentences. A further subtlety is that representing the meaning of each sentence alone is insufficient, since the relation can depend on links between lower-level elements like entity mentions.

Our approach computes distributional meaning representations by composition along the syntactic parse tree. Unlike prior work in compositional distributional semantics, we also compute representations for entity mentions through a novel downward compositional pass. Discourse relations are then predicted using both the distributional representations of the sentences and those of their coreferent entity mentions.

This system achieves substantial improvements over the previous state-of-the-art in predicting implicit discourse relations in the Penn Discourse Treebank.

(139 words)

input:
In this work, we propose a new method to integrate two recent lines of work:
unsupervised induction of shallow semantics (e.g., semantic roles) and
factorization of relations in text and knowledge bases. Our model consists of
two components: (1) an encoding component: a semantic role labeling model which
predicts roles given a rich set of syntactic and lexical features; (2) a
reconstruction component: a tensor factorization model which relies on roles to
predict argument fillers. When the components are estimated jointly to minimize
errors in argument reconstruction, the induced roles largely correspond to
roles defined in annotated resources. Our method performs on par with most
accurate role induction methods on English, even though, unlike these previous
approaches, we do not incorporate any prior linguistic knowledge about the
language.
Help me polish this: In this work, we propose a novel method that integrates two recent research directions: the unsupervised induction of shallow semantics (such as semantic roles) and the factorization of relations in text and knowledge bases. Our model comprises two components: (1) an encoder—a semantic role labeling model that predicts roles using rich syntactic and lexical features; and (2) a reconstructor—a tensor factorization model that uses these roles to predict argument fillers. When jointly optimized to minimize argument reconstruction error, the induced roles align closely with those defined in annotated resources. Despite incorporating no prior linguistic knowledge, our approach performs comparably to the most accurate role induction methods for English.

input:
The notion of metric plays a key role in machine learning problems such as
classification, clustering or ranking. However, it is worth noting that there
is a severe lack of theoretical guarantees that can be expected on the
generalization capacity of the classifier associated to a given metric. The
theoretical framework of $(\epsilon, \gamma, \tau)$-good similarity functions
(Balcan et al., 2008) has been one of the first attempts to draw a link between
the properties of a similarity function and those of a linear classifier making
use of it. In this paper, we extend and complete this theory by providing a new
generalization bound for the associated classifier based on the algorithmic
robustness framework.
Help me polish this:
The concept of a metric is central to many machine learning tasks, including classification, clustering, and ranking. Yet, there is a notable scarcity of theoretical guarantees regarding the generalization ability of a classifier built from a specific metric. The framework of $(\epsilon, \gamma, \tau)$-good similarity functions (Balcan et al., 2008) was a pioneering effort to formally connect the properties of a similarity function with the performance of a linear classifier that employs it. In this work, we extend and refine this theory by deriving a novel generalization bound for the associated classifier, grounded in the algorithmic robustness framework.

(Word count: 104)

input:
We present the multiplicative recurrent neural network as a general model for
compositional meaning in language, and evaluate it on the task of fine-grained
sentiment analysis. We establish a connection to the previously investigated
matrix-space models for compositionality, and show they are special cases of
the multiplicative recurrent net. Our experiments show that these models
perform comparably or better than Elman-type additive recurrent neural networks
and outperform matrix-space models on a standard fine-grained sentiment
analysis corpus. Furthermore, they yield comparable results to structural deep
models on the recently published Stanford Sentiment Treebank without the need
for generating parse trees.
Help me polish this:
We introduce the multiplicative recurrent neural network as a general model for compositional meaning in language, evaluating it on fine-grained sentiment analysis. We connect it to prior matrix-space models, demonstrating they are special cases of this architecture. Our experiments reveal that multiplicative recurrent nets match or surpass Elman-type additive recurrent networks and exceed matrix-space models on a standard sentiment corpus. Moreover, they achieve results comparable to structural deep models on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank, without requiring parse tree generation.

(Word count: 99)

input:
Finding minima of a real valued non-convex function over a high dimensional
space is a major challenge in science. We provide evidence that some such
functions that are defined on high dimensional domains have a narrow band of
values whose pre-image contains the bulk of its critical points. This is in
contrast with the low dimensional picture in which this band is wide. Our
simulations agree with the previous theoretical work on spin glasses that
proves the existence of such a band when the dimension of the domain tends to
infinity. Furthermore our experiments on teacher-student networks with the
MNIST dataset establish a similar phenomenon in deep networks. We finally
observe that both the gradient descent and the stochastic gradient descent
methods can reach this level within the same number of steps.
Help me polish this:
Locating the minima of a real-valued, non-convex function in a high-dimensional space is a significant scientific challenge. We present evidence that for certain such functions, the pre-image of a narrow band of values contains the majority of critical points. This contrasts with the low-dimensional case, where this band is wide. Our simulations align with prior theoretical work on spin glasses, which proves such a band exists as the domain's dimension approaches infinity.

Furthermore, experiments on teacher-student networks using the MNIST dataset reveal a similar phenomenon within deep neural networks. Finally, we observe that both gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent can converge to this value band in a comparable number of steps.

input:
We develop a new statistical model for photographic images, in which the
local responses of a bank of linear filters are described as jointly Gaussian,
with zero mean and a covariance that varies slowly over spatial position. We
optimize sets of filters so as to minimize the nuclear norms of matrices of
their local activations (i.e., the sum of the singular values), thus
encouraging a flexible form of sparsity that is not tied to any particular
dictionary or coordinate system. Filters optimized according to this objective
are oriented and bandpass, and their responses exhibit substantial local
correlation. We show that images can be reconstructed nearly perfectly from
estimates of the local filter response covariances alone, and with minimal
degradation (either visual or MSE) from low-rank approximations of these
covariances. As such, this representation holds much promise for use in
applications such as denoising, compression, and texture representation, and
may form a useful substrate for hierarchical decompositions.
Help me polish this:
We introduce a new statistical model for photographic images, in which the responses of a bank of linear filters are treated as jointly Gaussian with zero mean. A key feature is that the covariance of these responses varies slowly across spatial position. We optimize filter sets to minimize the nuclear norm (the sum of singular values) of their local activation matrices. This promotes a flexible form of sparsity independent of any fixed dictionary or coordinate system.

Filters optimized under this objective become oriented and bandpass, and their responses show strong local correlation. We demonstrate that images can be reconstructed almost perfectly using only estimates of these local covariance matrices. Even low-rank approximations of the covariances allow reconstruction with minimal visual or mean-squared-error degradation.

Consequently, this representation shows significant promise for applications including denoising, compression, and texture modeling. It may also serve as a useful foundation for hierarchical image decompositions.

(Word count: 156)

input:
Most modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs) used for object recognition
are built using the same principles: Alternating convolution and max-pooling
layers followed by a small number of fully connected layers. We re-evaluate the
state of the art for object recognition from small images with convolutional
networks, questioning the necessity of different components in the pipeline. We
find that max-pooling can simply be replaced by a convolutional layer with
increased stride without loss in accuracy on several image recognition
benchmarks. Following this finding -- and building on other recent work for
finding simple network structures -- we propose a new architecture that
consists solely of convolutional layers and yields competitive or state of the
art performance on several object recognition datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100,
ImageNet). To analyze the network we introduce a new variant of the
"deconvolution approach" for visualizing features learned by CNNs, which can be
applied to a broader range of network structures than existing approaches.
Help me polish this:
Most contemporary convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for object recognition follow a similar design: alternating convolution and max-pooling layers, topped with a few fully connected layers. This work re-examines the standard pipeline for object recognition from small images, questioning the need for each component. We discover that max-pooling can be replaced by a convolutional layer with an increased stride, with no loss of accuracy on standard benchmarks.

Building on this finding and other recent efforts to simplify network design, we introduce a new architecture composed exclusively of convolutional layers. This model achieves competitive, state-of-the-art performance on several object recognition datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet). To help interpret the network, we also present a novel variant of the "deconvolution method" for visualizing CNN-learned features. This approach is applicable to a wider range of network architectures than previous techniques.

(Word count: 156)

input:
Artificial neural networks typically have a fixed, non-linear activation
function at each neuron. We have designed a novel form of piecewise linear
activation function that is learned independently for each neuron using
gradient descent. With this adaptive activation function, we are able to
improve upon deep neural network architectures composed of static rectified
linear units, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 (7.51%),
CIFAR-100 (30.83%), and a benchmark from high-energy physics involving Higgs
boson decay modes.
Help me polish this:
Artificial neural networks traditionally use fixed, non-linear activation functions. We introduce a novel, learnable piecewise linear activation function that adapts independently for each neuron via gradient descent. This adaptive approach outperforms deep networks built with static rectified linear units, achieving state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10 (7.51% error), CIFAR-100 (30.83% error), and a Higgs boson decay benchmark from high-energy physics.

(Word count: 74)

input:
This paper introduces a greedy parser based on neural networks, which
leverages a new compositional sub-tree representation. The greedy parser and
the compositional procedure are jointly trained, and tightly depends on
each-other. The composition procedure outputs a vector representation which
